api/KeyTweening.KeyTweenScrollList.html.title: Class KeyTweenScrollList | KeyTween
api/KeyTweening.KeyTweenScrollList.html.summary: Class KeyTweenScrollList Namespace KeyTweening Assembly KeyTween.dll A virtualized list on a ScrollRect: only the visible items exist, and they are reused as the list scrolls. Laid out like Unity's Vertical / Horizontal / Grid Layout Group (plus Masonry), filled through callbacks like UI Toolkit's ListView (bind / unbind by index), and animated with the items' KeyTween states: an entry stagger, a state when scrolling brings an item into view, and a state scrubbed by the item's position. Also: several item prefabs, variable sizes, infinite loop, snapping / one page per swipe, auto scroll, sticky section headers, sticking to the end (chat), animated item resizing (accordion) and nested scrolling. api/KeyTweening.html.summary: Namespace KeyTweening Classes KeyTween Holds the animation states of one prefab and plays them. States can run at the same time; a newly played state takes over only the properties it animates. KeyTweenBinding KeyTweenChildCall Plays another KeyTween's state at a point in this state's time (e.g. a popup showing its buttons). KeyTweenColorTrack<T> A custom track of a Color. KeyTweenCustomTrack<T> A custom track on a component of type T. Override Get(T) and Set(T, Vector4); the value is a Vector4 (use x for one number, x/y for two …) as Kind says. [Preserve] public sealed class SliderHandleTrack : KeyTweenCustomTrack<Slider> { … } The class needs a public parameterless constructor. Mark it [UnityEngine.Scripting.Preserve] when the build strips code (IL2CPP with Managed Stripping Level above Minimal), because tracks are created from the saved class name. KeyTweenDefaultTransitions Default transitions, the same as UnityScreenNavigator's defaults: 0.3 s OutQuart. Pages slide by one screen width (Size Relative, so any resolution), modals grow from 0.3 and fade in, backdrops and sheets fade (Linear). KeyTweenEasing The easing formulas (easings.net, as in LitMotion's EaseUtility). KeyTweenEventAttribute Registers a struct as a custom animation event type. Its public fields become the event's parameters, edited per event in the KeyTween Editor; code receives them with anim.AddListener((in KeyTweenEventInfo e, in HitEvent hit) => ...). [KeyTweenEvent("Hit")] public struct HitEvent { public float damage; public string sfx; } Fields: numbers, bool, string, Vector2/3, Color, enums (stored as JSON, so no object references). KeyTweenEventListener Connects animation events to UnityEvents in the Inspector, so designers can react without code (e.g. "Shown" → AudioSource.PlayOneShot). Custom [KeyTweenEvent] struct data is for code: use KeyTween.AddListener<T>. KeyTweenEventListener.Binding KeyTweenEventMarker An animation event: a named point in a state's time, raised once when playback passes it (e.g. play a sound on impact). It can carry one custom KeyTweenEventAttribute struct, stored as JSON and converted once on first use. KeyTweenEventTrack A track of animation events (added like any other track). KeyTweenExternalProperties Track properties of components from optional packages (UIEffect …). The core lists them in KeyTweenProperty but does not reference those packages: each package's integration assembly (compiled only when the package is installed) registers how to read and write its properties. Unregistered ones (package not installed) are skipped. KeyTweenExternalProperties.Entry KeyTweenFloatTrack<T> A custom track of one number. e.g. class SliderValueTrack : KeyTweenFloatTrack<Slider>. KeyTweenKey A value at a time. Ease/curve describe how the track arrives at this key from the previous one. KeyTweenModalContainer Modals on top of each other. Each has its own backdrop (a dimmed full-screen image) that fades with it; the modal under the new one does not move. KeyTweenOverride A nested KeyTween's state changed inside this prefab only (e.g. the common button flashes differently in this popup). Only the changed tracks are stored, matched to the child's by target + property; every other track keeps following the child's own state, so later changes to the child prefab still show up here. Stored on the outer prefab, so the child's prefab is never touched; for the same track the outermost override wins. KeyTweenPageContainer A history of pages: Push puts a page on top (the old one leaves at the same time), Pop goes back. A page pushed with stack = false is dropped from the history once the next page is in (e.g. a loading page). KeyTweenPageIndicator Dots or tabs for a scroll list's items (pages, banners, tab pages): one item per list item, laid out by this object's layout group. The current one plays the On state and the one it replaces plays Off. Clicking one scrolls there. KeyTweenPlay A play of one state, set up in code before it starts (With(string)): a track's end value or arrival, where it starts, callbacks. Nothing changes until it plays; the changes hold for that play only (put back when it completes or is canceled), and the same object can be played again and again, like a LitMotion builder you keep. KeyTweenPullToRefresh Pull to refresh on a list: pulling past the start shows the Pull state by distance; releasing past Distance raises On Refresh and plays the Refreshing state (repeated) until EndRefresh(), holding the list open meanwhile. For vertical lists (pulled down from the top). KeyTweenScreen A page, modal or sheet shown by a screen container. Its transitions are states of its KeyTween, by name: pages "PushEnter", "PushExit", "PopEnter", "PopExit"; modals "Enter", "Exit"; sheets "Enter", "Exit" (and optionally "EnterBackward", "ExitBackward"). A missing one uses the container's default. KeyTweenScreenContainer Shared by the page, modal and sheet containers: taps are off on every container while any of them is in a transition (so a second tap cannot start another one), and screens get their default transitions from here. KeyTweenScrollList A virtualized list on a ScrollRect: only the visible items exist, and they are reused as the list scrolls. Laid out like Unity's Vertical / Horizontal / Grid Layout Group (plus Masonry), filled through callbacks like UI Toolkit's ListView (bind / unbind by index), and animated with the items' KeyTween states: an entry stagger, a state when scrolling brings an item into view, and a state scrubbed by the item's position. Also: several item prefabs, variable sizes, infinite loop, snapping / one page per swipe, auto scroll, sticky section headers, sticking to the end (chat), animated item resizing (accordion) and nested scrolling. KeyTweenScrollScrub Shows a state by how far a list is scrolled instead of by time: 0 px = the state's start, Distance = its end (a header that collapses as the list scrolls, a toolbar that fades in). KeyTweenSharedElement Shared element transitions: an image on one screen appears to travel to (or from) where it sits on another screen. The motion is a normal state (AnchoredPosition + SizeDelta tracks on the moving image, edited in the window); only the other screen's end is known at run time, so this writes it into the state's first or last keys just before the state plays. KeyTweenSheetContainer Sheets (tab pages) without history: Show switches to one, the old one leaves at the same time. Moving to a lower index plays "EnterBackward" / "ExitBackward" when the sheet has them (e.g. slide the other way). KeyTweenSound A sound played once when playback passes its time, through the KeyTween's AudioSource. KeyTweenSoundTrack A track of sounds played through source (empty = the KeyTween's AudioSource). KeyTweenState KeyTweenStateBuilder A state made in code (Build(string)): tracks and keys, events, sounds and callbacks, added to the KeyTween as a runtime state (not saved) and played by name like one made in the editor. Add() adds it; the Play methods add it and play it. Calls after that keep editing the same state. KeyTweenTrack KeyTweenTrackType What a track animates: which component it needs, how to read and write the value, and how the editor shows it. The built-in tracks are instances of this class; a custom track derives from KeyTweenCustomTrack<T> (or KeyTweenFloatTrack<T>, KeyTweenVector2Track<T>, KeyTweenVector3Track<T>, KeyTweenColorTrack<T>) and then appears in the Add Track window for objects that have T. KeyTweenTrackTypes Finds the type of a track: built-in by its KeyTweenProperty, custom by its saved class name. KeyTweenTrigger Plays KeyTween states when UI events happen on this object. KeyTweenVector2Track<T> A custom track of a Vector2. KeyTweenVector3Track<T> A custom track of a Vector3. Structs KeyTweenEventInfo What an animation event handler receives (like Unity 6.5's AnimationEventInfo): passed by in, no allocation. KeyTweenTransition What a screen gets in its lifecycle calls. Interfaces IKeyTweenScreenLifecycle Implement on any component of a screen's root to run code around its transitions. The Will* calls are awaited before the animation starts (load data, preload the next screen); the Did* calls come after it ends. Enums KeyTweenCurveType KeyTweenEase How a key arrives. Same members, order and formulas as LitMotion's Ease, so data saved with LitMotion.Ease (an int) reads back unchanged. KeyTweenEvent KeyTweenProperty KeyTweenScramble Characters a Text Reveal track shows where text is not revealed yet. Same values as LitMotion's ScrambleMode. KeyTweenScrollList.Alignment KeyTweenScrollList.GridConstraint KeyTweenScrollList.LayoutType KeyTweenScrollList.SnapMode KeyTweenStart Where a track's first key gets its value when the state starts. KeyTweenTimeMode Which clock a KeyTween plays on, like Animator's Update Mode. KeyTweenTransitionKind Why a screen is entering or leaving. KeyTweenValueKind How a track's value is edited and how many of its four numbers (x, y, z, w) it uses. Delegates KeyTweenEventHandler KeyTweenEventHandler<T>

articles/changelog.html.summary: Changelog All notable changes to this package are documented here. The format follows Keep a Changelog and the package uses Semantic Versioning. [0.3.0] - 2026-10-31 Play from a given time and stop at a time, start and end callbacks per state, With to set up a play in code and Build to make a state in code, and the same for UniTask and R3. Sample is deprecated (use Stop(state, time)). Added Play from a given time: Play(state, time), PlayAsync(state, time, token), PlayReversed(state, time), PlayReversedAsync(state, time, token). Time is in seconds on the state's timeline; the pose at that time is written at once, and events, sounds and child calls before it are not raised. Stop(state, time): stops the state if it is playing (a pending PlayAsync is canceled) and shows its pose at that time, without playing. Start and end callbacks per state: On Start, On Complete and On Cancel (UnityEvents in the state settings of the KeyTween Editor, saved in the prefab), and the component events StateStarted, StateCompleted, StateCanceled (with the state's name). Each play starts with On Start and ends with exactly one of the other two, at the same moments as PlayAsync completes or is canceled. The editor preview and Stop(state, time) on a state that is not playing call none. With(state): set up a play in code and play it (.Play(), .PlayAsync(), …): the end value or arrival of a track's last key (WithEndValue, WithEase, WithCurve, WithPunch, WithShake; built-in, Material and custom tracks), the start time (WithTime, WithEventsBefore), callbacks for that play (WithOnStart, WithOnComplete, WithOnCancel, WithOnLoop). The changes hold for that play only, and the returned KeyTweenPlay can be kept and played again without allocating. Build(state): make a state in code (Track, Key, KeyCurve, KeyPunch, KeyShake, From, Event, Sound, Loop, OnStart / OnComplete / OnCancel), then Add() it as a runtime state or play it at once. UniTask integration: PlayUniTaskAsync / PlayReversedUniTaskAsync from a given time, and on a With play (KeyTweenPlay). R3 integration: PlayAsObservable(state, time), PlayAsObservable on a With play, and StateStartedAsObservable / StateCompletedAsObservable / StateCanceledAsObservable. Changed A play is marked as playing before its first events: an event at the start (or On Start) that calls Stop on the state now stops it, and its PlayAsync is canceled. Fixed AddState replacing a playing state of the same name left its timer running and its PlayAsync waiting; it stops it now (the PlayAsync is canceled). KeyTween Editor: after moving or stretching keys, the stretch handles could stay hidden until the selection changed (they waited for a layout signal that did not always come). A looping child state whose tracks an outer prefab overrides played once instead of looping (the merged state lost Loop). With(...).WithEndValue(...).PlayReversed() ignored the end value once the state had played forward (a reversed play reuses the last forward play's values); the end value given for the reversed play is used now. Playing a state with child calls allocated on every play (looking up the ancestors' overrides for the length). It allocates nothing now, unless an outer prefab overrides the called child's tracks. KeyTween Editor: Add KeyTween to '…' appeared only for UI objects (RectTransform); it appears for any selected object now, as the non-UI tracks need. Deprecated Sample(state, time): use Stop(state, time), which does the same. Sample will be removed in the next version. The package and its samples use Stop now. [0.2.1] - 2026-10-29 KeyTween Editor: copy and paste keys, state tabs you can rename, duplicate and reorder, stretch handles for selected keys. The runtime and playback are unchanged. Added KeyTween Editor: copy and paste keys (Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V on the timeline, or the context menu). Pasted at the playhead (or where you right-click, Paste Keys Here, also after the end) with their spacing, onto the track of the same object and kind (made when missing); in another prefab, onto the object at the same path from the root. KeyTween Editor: state tabs can be renamed (double-click), duplicated, reordered (drag, or Move Left / Right) and deleted from the tab (right-click). A state is not renamed to an empty name or one another state has. KeyTween Editor: selecting two or more keys at different times shows a box around them with a handle at each end. Dragging a handle stretches or shrinks the selected keys around the other end, like the Animation window. Removed KeyTween Editor: the key inspector's Capture Current Value button. Record (●) puts what you change in the scene into keys. Fixed KeyTween Editor: a box selection can start anywhere in the key area (the event and child call lanes, the empty space below the last track), like the Animation window. Before, it started only on a track's lane, so dragging from below the tracks did nothing. [0.2.0] - 2026-10-28 Tracks for game objects (not only UI), custom tracks, and playback that follows Time.timeScale. KeyTweens that must keep moving while the game is paused (timeScale 0), such as a pause menu, need Time set to Unscaled (see Changed). Added Documentation site: https://unialgames.github.io/KeyTween/ (the documents and an API reference). The Package Manager's Documentation link opens it, and the READMEs link to it. README and API document: awaiting several KeyTweens together (PlayAsync in turn, Task.WhenAll, UniTask.WhenAll). Tracks for objects that are not UI: Position, World Position, World Rotation (Transform), Color and Alpha (SpriteRenderer), Material tracks for a Renderer's color, number and vector properties (through a MaterialPropertyBlock, the material asset is not changed), Light (Color, Intensity, Range, Spot Angle), Camera (Field of View, Near Clip, Far Clip, Viewport Rect) and AudioSource (Volume, Pitch). UI tracks: Offset Min and Max (RectTransform), UV Rect (RawImage), Effect Color and Distance (Shadow, Outline), Softness and Padding (RectMask2D), Value (Slider), Scroll Position (ScrollRect), Min, Preferred and Flexible Size (LayoutElement). TextMeshPro tracks: Word Spacing, Line Spacing, Outline Width, Outline Color, Face Dilate, Underlay Color. Material tracks use an instance of the text's material; the editor preview puts the original back. Custom tracks: derive from KeyTweenFloatTrack<T> (or the Vector2, Vector3, Color and Vector4 versions) and implement Get and Set; the track appears in the Add Track window for objects with T. Changed Playback now follows Time.timeScale by default, like Animator, DOTween and LitMotion: pausing the game (timeScale 0) pauses KeyTween animations. Each KeyTween has Time (timeMode): Scaled (default) or Unscaled (real time, the old behavior, for pause menus and loading screens). It is a normal serialized field, so a prefab instance can override it. Existing prefabs load as Scaled; set the ones that must move while paused to Unscaled. When states overlap, a new state takes over the shared channels of another kind of track on the same value: an Alpha state takes only the a of a playing Color track, which keeps writing r, g, b; a Color state stops a playing Alpha track. The same holds for Char Color and Char Alpha, and Offset Min/Max take over Position and Size. The Add Track window offers Sound only on the root. A sound track still picks its AudioSource in its inspector (Audio Source (optional)). Recording puts a change on a track the state already has for that field: World Position, World Rotation, Offset Min/Max, a SpriteRenderer's Alpha, Scroll Position (moving the Content) and Number (the number in the text). Before, it made a second Position, Rotation, Size or Color track. Editing a text no longer records a Reveal key. Light, Camera, AudioSource, Shadow, LayoutElement and UIEffect values are recorded too. Each track kind is defined in one place (KeyTweenTrackType): reading, writing, the editor's field, preview restore and recording. KeyTween.Read and KeyTween.Write still work for built-in properties. [0.1.3] - 2026-10-27 Changed README: the install URL without a tag follows the latest release (update with Update in the Package Manager); a new section explains installing a specific version (#v0.1.3), which Update does not move. [0.1.2] - 2026-10-27 Simpler play API. Code that passed KeyTweenInterrupt or called PlayState needs a small change (below). Changed A state that is played takes the properties it animates from states already playing, where they are, and continues from there; a state left with no properties stops (its PlayAsync is canceled). This was the default (KeyTweenInterrupt.Cancel) and is now the only behavior. Play(string) and PlayReversed(string) take one argument, so they are listed for UnityEvents such as a Button's OnClick. Play(string, PointerEventData) passes the pointer for tracks that start from it. Removed KeyTweenInterrupt, the interrupt parameter of Play, PlayAsync, PlayReversed, PlayReversedAsync, PlayUniTaskAsync, PlayReversedUniTaskAsync and PlayAsObservable, and the Interrupt setting of Play On. To finish a state before the next one, call Complete("state") first: its end pose, its remaining events, its await completing. PlayState and PlayStateReversed: use Play and PlayReversed. UnityEvents saved with the old names must be picked again (the samples are updated). [0.1.1] - 2026-10-27 Fixed Importing a sample into a project without TMP Essential Resources left every label invisible. KeyTween now imports them automatically when a sample is imported into such a project (the same as Window › TextMeshPro › Import TMP Essential Resources). [0.1.0] - 2026-10-23 First public release. Added KeyTween component: keyframe states stored in the prefab (no clip or controller assets), each a set of tracks on the prefab's own components. KeyTween Editor window: state tabs, timeline with tracks and keys, Add Track window, key inspector, recording (●), animation event and sound tracks, child prefab state calls. Live preview in Edit, Prefab and Play mode; values return when the preview stops. Saving: Auto Save and Save (Ctrl+S); edits made on running copies in Play mode are written back to the source prefab. Tracks: scale, rotation, position, size, anchors, pivot, active, color, alpha, CanvasGroup alpha, fill, camera, TMP font size, character spacing, typewriter reveal, number count-up, and per-character scale, position, rotation, color and alpha. Arrival: 36 eases, AnimationCurve, Punch and Shake. Nested prefabs: a parent state calls a child prefab's state and overrides its tracks in the current prefab only. Play On triggers: OnEnable, Start, pointer enter/exit/down/up, click, select/deselect, toggle on/off. API: Play, PlayAsync (Unity Awaitable), PlayReversed, Complete, Stop, Sample, SetEndValue, animation events. Scroll list: virtualized list, grid, masonry, carousel, infinite loop, pages, banners, wheel picker, section headers, chat and accordion layouts. Screen transitions: Page, Modal and Sheet containers with lifecycle callbacks and shared element transitions. Performance: no cost while idle, no GC allocation while playing, eased tracks evaluated in batches with Burst. Optional integrations, enabled when installed: UniTask, R3, UIEffect. Samples: RPG Sample, UI Components.

articles/en/adding-tracks.html.title: Adding Tracks | KeyTween
articles/en/adding-tracks.html.summary: Adding Tracks A track animates one property of one object. You choose tracks in the Add Track window and add them to the state. Opening the Add Track Window Right-click an empty part of the timeline and choose Add Track.... Choosing Tracks The left side of the Add Track window shows the object tree of the prefab. The right side shows the track cards available for the selected object, along with their current values. Select an object in the tree on the left. You can search the tree. Click track cards on the right to select them. You can select several. Click Add N. Double-click a card to add it immediately. Your selection is kept while you move between objects. Tracks that already exist are marked Added. Defaults for New Tracks A new track gets a key at 0 s and a key at the state's end time. Both keys hold the current value. If the state is empty, the end key is placed at 0.2 s. Start is Current Value. Only Reveal and per-character tracks start with Key Value. The end key arrives with the Ease OutSine. A new per-character track's Stagger is 0.05 s. For the Start option, see Track Options. Available Tracks The Add Track window shows only the tracks that match the components on the selected object. Objects Target Tracks Any object Scale, Rotation, Active Objects that are not UI (Transform) Position, World Position, World Rotation UI Target Tracks RectTransform Position, Size, Anchor Min, Anchor Max, Pivot, Offset Min, Offset Max CanvasGroup Group Alpha Graphic (Image, RawImage, TMP, and so on) Color, Alpha Image (Image Type = Filled) Fill Amount RawImage UV Rect Shadow, Outline Effect Color, Effect Distance RectMask2D Softness, Padding Slider Value ScrollRect Scroll Position LayoutElement Min Size, Preferred Size, Flexible Size TextMeshPro Target Tracks TMP_Text Font Size, Character Spacing, Word Spacing, Line Spacing, Reveal (Typewriter), Number (Count) TMP_Text material Outline Width, Outline Color, Face Dilate, Underlay Color TMP_Text per character Char Scale, Char Position, Char Rotation, Char Color, Char Alpha 2D, 3D, camera and sound Target Tracks SpriteRenderer Color, Alpha Renderer (MeshRenderer and so on) Material tracks: one per color, number and vector property of its material (e.g. Material _BaseColor) Light Light Color, Intensity, Range (Point, Spot), Spot Angle (Spot) Camera Camera Background, Camera Size, Field of View, Near Clip, Far Clip, Viewport Rect AudioSource Volume, Pitch Events and sounds Target Tracks Root Animation Events, Sound Other tracks With UIEffect installed, 14 UIEffect tracks are added. For details, see Integrations. You can write your own track for a component of your project. For details, see Custom Tracks. Things to know Group Alpha is for fading a whole screen or popup. Rotation and World Rotation use Euler angles in degrees. Values are read in the range −180 to 180, so going from −30° to 0° does not turn the long way around. Active does not interpolate between keys. It turns the object on or off at each key's time. Material tracks write through a MaterialPropertyBlock. The material asset does not change, and other objects that use the same material are not affected. TMP material tracks make a material instance used only by that text. When the preview stops, the original material comes back. Changing a Track's Target To change a track's target, click the path · property ▾ button at the top of the track inspector.

articles/en/animation-events.html.title: Animation Events | KeyTween
articles/en/animation-events.html.summary: Animation Events You can receive, in code, the events placed on an event track in the editor. An event is raised when a play passes its time. Defining an Event Data Type A struct marked with [KeyTweenEvent] appears in the editor's event type list. [KeyTweenEvent("Popup Sound")] public struct PopupSoundEvent { public string clip; public float volume; } Public fields are saved as JSON. Object references cannot be saved. The type list shows only structs that are included in the player build. Receiving All Events event KeyTweenEventHandler EventRaised is raised when a play passes an event. Complete raises the skipped events in order; a cancel raises none. anim.EventRaised += (in KeyTweenEventInfo e) => Debug.Log($"{e.State}:{e.Name} @ {e.Time}"); Receiving Events by Data Type AddListener<T> receives only events whose data type is T. Call Dispose on the returned IDisposable to remove the listener. using var sub = anim.AddListener<PopupSoundEvent>((in KeyTweenEventInfo e, in PopupSoundEvent data) => Play(data.clip)); Waiting for an Event WaitEventAsync completes the next time an event with that name is raised, from any state. It returns Awaitable<KeyTweenEventInfo>. var info = await anim.WaitEventAsync("Shown"); Reading Event Info KeyTweenEventInfo is a readonly struct, passed with in. It provides the following members. Member Type What it is Animation KeyTween The KeyTween that raised the event State string The name of the state that was playing Name string The event's name Time float The event's time in the state, in seconds TryGetData<T>(out T) bool If the event's data is a T, gets it and returns true Use TryGetData when one handler deals with events of several data types. anim.EventRaised += (in KeyTweenEventInfo e) => { if (e.TryGetData(out PopupSoundEvent sound)) audio.PlayOneShot(Load(sound.clip), sound.volume); else if (e.Name == "Shown") EnableInput(); }; Receiving Events Without Code The KeyTweenEventListener component receives events without code. Add Add Component > KeyTween > Event Listener. Connect event names to UnityEvents. The event data is not passed in this case.

articles/en/arrival.html.title: Arrival | KeyTween
articles/en/arrival.html.summary: Arrival A key sets only when (its time) and what value. How the track gets from one key to the next is its arrival. When you open a drawer, you pull it fast at first and slow down as it comes out: moving the same distance in the same time feels completely different depending on how the speed changes on the way. The three lines in the graph have the same keys: 0 at 0 s and 1 at the end. Only the arrival differs. One per Key, for the Segment Coming In Each key has one arrival, and it sets how the track moves from the previous key to this key. With three keys there are two segments, and each can use a different arrival. The segment from key 1 to key 2 uses key 2's arrival, and the one from key 2 to key 3 uses key 3's. The first key has no segment coming in, so its arrival is disabled. The exception is a track whose Start is Current Value with only one key: the segment from the value at play time to that key uses that key's arrival. Choosing It in the Editor Select a key on the timeline. In the key inspector's Arrival section, choose a Type. Set the fields for that Type. The graph below updates at once, showing how the track goes from the previous key's value (lower line) to this key's value (upper line). Type Fields Use it for Ease Ease (36 curves) Most animations: pick a ready-made curve Curve Animation Curve A shape no ease has: draw it yourself Punch Ease, Frequency, Damping A bump that springs back into place Shake Ease, Frequency, Damping A random jitter that settles back into place With several keys selected, only the Arrival section is shown, and it changes all of them at once. A field whose value differs between the keys shows —. Check the result right away with the ▶ preview. Ease: Picking a Ready-Made Curve The most used Type. Choose one of 36 curves. The two parts of a name mean: Part Meaning In / Out / InOut Where it is slow. In starts slowly and speeds up. Out starts fast and arrives slowly. InOut is slow at both ends Sine → Quad → Cubic → Quart → Quint → Expo How strong the change is. Further right, the gap between the slow and fast parts grows Circ A circular arc Back Goes slightly back before starting (In), or slightly past the target before coming back (Out) Elastic Wobbles like a rubber band Bounce Arrives as if bouncing off the floor The first 32, Linear through InOutBounce, match LitMotion's Ease in number and formula. OutBackQuad through OutBackQuint are Unity-AnimationUI's OutBack family. Each goes further past the target before coming back. CustomAnimationCurve as an Ease is the same as Linear. To draw a curve yourself, choose the Curve Type. Choosing an Ease for UI There is no single right answer, but starting from these usually looks natural. Animation Try first Why Entering the screen, opening a popup OutCubic, OutQuart Appears quickly and settles softly, so it feels responsive Leaving the screen, closing InCubic, InQuad Starts slowly and disappears fast, so the exit does not linger From one place to another (tab switch, slide) InOutSine, InOutCubic Soft at both the start and the end A button press, a popup that pops out OutBack Goes slightly past and comes back, so it feels springy Falling and landing OutBounce Shows the bounce off the floor Counting a number, a progress bar Linear, OutQuad A constant speed, or slowing slightly only at the end Repeating breathing or pulsing (Loop) InOutSine The speed is 0 at both ends, so the laps join without a break Curve: Drawing Your Own If no ease has the shape you want, choose the Curve Type, click the Animation Curve field and draw it in Unity's curve editor. The horizontal axis is the progress through the segment: 0 at the previous key's time, 1 at this key's time. The vertical axis is the value: 0 at the previous key's value, 1 at this key's value. Above 1 or below 0, the track goes past the target or the other way and comes back. Usually put the end point at (1, 1), so the track reaches this key's value exactly at this key's time. Punch and Shake: Shaking and Settling Back Use these for a bump when a button is pressed, or a jitter on an error. Unlike the other Types, this key's value is not a destination but the strength of the shake. The value shakes around the previous key's value and, when the segment ends, comes back to the previous key's value. Punch goes back and forth at a steady beat. Shake jitters randomly on each axis every frame. Field Meaning New key Strength (the key's value) How big the shake is, per axis. The example above shakes up to 15 degrees on Z — Frequency How fast it shakes. Higher shakes more often. The same value as LitMotion's frequency 10 Damping How much the shake dies out. 1 dies out toward the end; 0 keeps the same strength until it returns into place 1 Ease How the shake is spread over time. With Out Sine, the shakes crowd toward the start and slow down later Out Sine The formulas are the same as LitMotion's LMotion.Punch and LMotion.Shake. Because it settles back into place, a Punch key usually comes right after a key at rest. For example, a key at 0 s (Scale 1) followed by a Punch key at 0.3 s (Strength 0.2) bumps around scale 1 and comes back to 1. Changing It in Code To change the arrival on a particular play, use With. The change holds for that play only and goes back to the editor's value when it ends. It changes the track's last key (the segment that arrives at the end value). anim.With("Open").WithEase(panel, KeyTweenProperty.Scale, KeyTweenEase.OutBack).Play(); anim.With("Hit").WithShake(icon, KeyTweenProperty.AnchoredPosition, frequency: 20f, damping: 0.5f).Play(); When you make a state in code, set it per key with Key(time, value, ease), KeyCurve, KeyPunch and KeyShake. For details, see the API. Notes On a track whose Start is Current Value, the first segment starts from the value at play time. The arrival applies the same way. Tracks that switch on and off, such as Active, have no in-between values. They change right at the key's time. While playing, tracks that use only Ease are computed together with Burst. Tracks with Curve, Punch or Shake keys are computed in regular code. It makes a difference only when hundreds play at once. For details, see Performance.

articles/en/awaiting-several.html.title: Awaiting Several KeyTweens | KeyTween
articles/en/awaiting-several.html.summary: Awaiting Several KeyTweens This section shows how to play KeyTween components on several objects at once and wait until all of them have finished. Starting All, Then Awaiting Each PlayAsync returns a Unity Awaitable, not a .NET Task, so you cannot pass it to Task.WhenAll directly. However, each play starts as soon as PlayAsync is called. If you start them all first and then await them one by one, the result is the same as WhenAll. var plays = anims.Select(a => a.PlayAsync("Hover")).ToList(); // all of them start here, at the same time foreach (var play in plays) await play; // wait until every one has ended Awaiting with Task.WhenAll To use Task.WhenAll, wrap each play in a Task. static async Task AsTask(Awaitable awaitable) => await awaitable; await Task.WhenAll(anims.Select(a => AsTask(a.PlayAsync("Hover")))); Awaiting with UniTask.WhenAll If UniTask is installed, you can use PlayUniTaskAsync from the integrations. await UniTask.WhenAll(anims.Select(a => a.PlayUniTaskAsync("Hover"))); When One Play Is Canceled If any of the plays is canceled (How a Play Ends), an OperationCanceledException is thrown. Where it is thrown depends on the approach. Starting all, then awaiting each: at the await of the canceled play Task.WhenAll, UniTask.WhenAll: at WhenAll

articles/en/build.html.title: Making a State in Code | KeyTween
articles/en/build.html.summary: Making a State in Code States are usually made in the editor, but you can also make one in code alone. Use this when the targets are known only at runtime, or for a small animation you do not want to make in the editor. Stack tracks and keys with Build(state), then add the state with Add, or add and play it with one of the Play methods. anim.Build("Pop") .Track(button.transform, KeyTweenProperty.Scale) // starts a track; the Keys until the next Track go on it .Key(0f, Vector3.one) .Key(0.15f, Vector3.one * 1.2f, KeyTweenEase.OutBack) // the segment arriving at this key uses OutBack .Key(0.3f, Vector3.one, KeyTweenEase.InOutSine) .Track(label, KeyTweenProperty.GraphicAlpha) .Key(0f, 0f).Key(0.2f, 1f) .Event(0.15f, "Peak") .OnComplete(() => Debug.Log("popped")) .Play(); Method What it does Track(target, property) Starts a track of a built-in property. A Material track is Track(renderer, "_BaseColor"), a custom track Track<MyTrack>(target) From(start) The track's Start. KeyTweenStart.KeyValue (the first key) by default; KeyTweenStart.Current (the value when it plays) or KeyTweenStart.Pointer Key(time, value, ease) One key. ease is how the segment arriving at this key moves (OutSine by default, as in the editor). The value is a Vector4 or a float; a Vector3, Vector2 or Color works too KeyCurve(time, value, curve), KeyPunch(time, strength, frequency = 10, damping = 1), KeyShake(...) A key whose arrival is Curve, Punch or Shake. The value is a Vector4 (a Vector3, Vector2 or Color works too); for Punch and Shake it is the strength of the shake, not a place to arrive at Event(time, name), Sound(time, clip, volume) An animation event and a sound Loop() Makes it a looping state OnStart, OnComplete, OnCancel The state's callbacks (every play of it) Add() Adds the state. Then play it by name, as in anim.Play("Pop") Play(), PlayAsync(), PlayReversed(), PlayReversedAsync() Adds it and plays it With() Adds it and goes on to set up a play (With) The state exists only at runtime. It is not saved, and you can use Play, Stop, Complete and With with it like a state made in the editor. Keys are placed in time order whatever order you add them in. A state with the same name is replaced. If that state is playing, it stops and its pending PlayAsync is canceled. Calling Key before Track throws right away. Adding a State Object You can also make a KeyTweenState yourself and add it with AddState. Build uses this method, and so do screen containers when they add their default transitions (Screens). public void AddState(KeyTweenState state); Use it where you already have a state object. For example, a default transition can be added to another screen under a name: var fade = KeyTweenDefaultTransitions.FadeIn(screen); fade.name = "FadeIn"; screen.Animation.AddState(fade); screen.Animation.Play("FadeIn"); A state with the same name is replaced. If that state is playing, it stops and its On Cancel is called. To base a state on another KeyTween's state, add a copy made with state.Clone(). One object added in two places changes in both when one is edited. The copy's tracks still point at the original targets (components).

articles/en/comparison.html.title: Comparison | KeyTween
articles/en/comparison.html.summary: Comparison This page compares the steps needed to build the same effect with each tool. Every comparison is based on work actually done in this repository. Benchmarks/Assets/Bench/*Driver.cs: code that implements the same three effects (pulse, list entry and text wave) with each method Assets/Reference: recreations of the Unity-AnimationUI and UnityScreenNavigator demos Assets/KeyTween/Samples/RPG: the RPG sample For the other tools, only the features used in this work are described. Features that were not tried are marked "Not checked". Performance is covered separately on the Performance page. 1. Making one effect — button pulse (scale + color, looping) This section uses a pulse effect, in which a button's scale and color change repeatedly, to compare the authoring steps and the code needed to run it with each tool. At a Glance Tool Made in Code to run KeyTween KeyTween window 0 lines (1 line from code) Animator Animation window + Animator window 0 lines (default state) DOTween Pro Inspector (DOTweenAnimation) or code 2 lines LitMotion Code 2 statements (4 lines) AnimationUI Inspector (AnimationUI sequence list) 1 line to loop Making It with KeyTween The effect is made in the KeyTween window. Add KeyTween to the button. Make a state "Pulse" and turn on Loop. Pick Scale and Color in the Add Track picker. Add keys at 0 / 0.5 / 1 s and set the ease to InOutSine. Set Play On to OnEnable. The state plays when the object is enabled, so the code to run is 0 lines. From code, it takes 1 line. anim.Play("Pulse"); States, Tracks and Keys in KeyTween These are the three concepts used in the steps above. State: one named effect Track: a row in the state that changes a single value such as scale or color Key: the value at a point in time on a track Creating states, adding tracks and editing keys all happen in the KeyTween window shown below. Making It with Animator The effect is made in the Animation window and the Animator window. Click Create in the Animation window. This creates 2 assets: a clip and a controller. Record the keys with Record. Check the clip's Loop Time. Check the default state in the controller. The default state plays on its own, so the code to run is 0 lines. To switch to another effect, use states and transitions, or call Play. Making It with DOTween Pro The effect is made in the inspector (DOTweenAnimation) or in code. Inspector: Add one component per effect (1 for scale + 1 for color). Set Loops to −1 and Yoyo. Code: The 2 lines below. DOScale(...).SetLoops(-1, Yoyo) DOColor(...)... Making It with LitMotion The effect is made in code only. You create one Motion per value and bind it to the target, and the whole pulse takes 2 statements (4 lines). The scale part looks like this. LMotion.Create(...).WithLoops(-1, Yoyo).BindToLocalScale(rt) Making It with AnimationUI Add steps to the AnimationUI sequence list in the inspector. Scale and color step Wait Step back Wait There is no loop feature, so looping takes 1 line of code. OnAnimationEnded += Play 2. Work per effect In the benchmark project, every method was implemented in code so that all of them could be measured under the same conditions. In real use, however, the difference that matters is whether an effect can be made in the editor. Where Each Effect Is Made The table shows where and how each effect is made with each tool. Effect KeyTween Animator DOTween Pro LitMotion AnimationUI Looping pulse Editor (window) Editor (window) Inspector or 2 lines of code 2 statements of code Inspector (4-step sequence) + 1 line of loop code List entry (current position → 0) Editor, Start = Current Value Editor, start value fixed in the clip 2 lines of code (From) 2 statements of code Inspector Text wave (per character) Editor (Char track + Stagger) Not possible Code: DOTweenTMPAnimator + a loop over the characters Code: a loop of BindToTMPCharPositionY per character Not possible Counting a number (currency) Editor (Number track) + 1 line for the end value (With(...).WithEndValue) Not checked Code Code Not possible Shared element transition Editor (state) + 1 line for the partner's keys (KeyTweenSharedElement) Not checked Code Code Not possible UIEffect values (dissolve etc.) Editor (14 UIEffect tracks) Editor (records serialized fields) Code (DOTween.To) Code (Bind) Not possible 3. Feature comparison (what was checked in this repository) Only features checked directly in this repository are listed. Symbols in the Table ✅: supported ❌: not supported Not checked: a feature that was not tried Feature Table Feature KeyTween Animator DOTween Pro LitMotion AnimationUI Keyframe editing in the editor ✅ Timeline window ✅ Animation window Inspector values (not keyframes) ❌ (separate packages not checked) Sequence list (start, duration) Recording ✅ ● (Scene/Inspector changes → keys) ✅ Record ❌ ❌ ❌ Preview in Edit mode ✅ Play, scrub, loop ✅ Not checked ❌ Not checked Keeping values changed in Play mode ✅ Auto Save · Save Edits in the Animation window are kept ❌ ❌ Not checked Start from the current value ✅ Start = Current Value ❌ (clip values) ✅ when From is omitted ✅ ❌ Reverse play ✅ PlayReversed (a current-value start also returns to its original place) Speed −1 (parameter) ✅ PlayBackwards Not checked ✅ PlayReversed Loop ✅ State Loop ✅ Loop Time ✅ ✅ ❌ (Play again) Per character ✅ Editor ❌ Code Code ❌ Event and sound tracks ✅ Events ✅ Callbacks (code) Callbacks (code) ✅ Event and sound steps Screen transition containers ✅ Page, Modal, Sheet ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌ await ✅ Awaitable, UniTask optional ❌ ✅ (AsyncWaitForCompletion) ✅ ❌ Start and end callbacks ✅ Editor (the state's Callbacks) + code (StateCompleted and so on, WithOnComplete) Not checked Code (OnComplete and so on) Code (WithOnComplete and so on) Not checked Making an effect in code ✅ Build(state).Track(...).Key(...) Not checked ✅ The usual way ✅ The usual way Not checked Playing from a given time ✅ Play(state, time) Not checked Not checked Not checked Not checked Time that ignores pausing ✅ Time = Unscaled ✅ Update Mode Not checked Not checked Not checked Required packages Unity packages only (uGUI, Mathematics, Burst) Built in DOTween (Pro is paid) LitMotion (+ Burst, Collections) AnimationUI source 4. Work when changing it This section compares the work needed to change an effect that already exists. Work per Change "Code tweens" refers to libraries such as DOTween and LitMotion, in which effects are written in code. What to change KeyTween Code tweens (DOTween, LitMotion) Animator Duration and ease Drag keys or pick an ease in the window, preview at once Edit code → compile → check in Play mode Move keys in the Animation window (ease through curve tangents) Adding an effect Add one state Add methods and fields Add a clip, a state and transitions Slightly different per prefab Child state override (in the current prefab) Branch in code or expose values Override Controller Designers do it themselves ✅ No code ❌ (partly possible with the DOTween Pro inspector) ✅ 5. Summary This section sums up each tool and the performance comparison. KeyTween You build effects in the KeyTween window without writing code, and you can preview them immediately. The following features used to require a code tween and are also available in the editor. Starting from the current value Per-character effects await What changes from play to play (the end value, the ease, the start time, callbacks) is set in code with With, and Build makes a state in code alone. So the code-first style of a code tween is there too. Performance The own cost of 2,000 pulses was compared in an IL2CPP build. The own cost is the time a method takes beyond setting the same values directly from a script. KeyTween: +0.38ms DOTween Pro: +0.40ms LitMotion: +0.34ms Animator: +2.85ms AnimationUI: +2.00ms KeyTween is on par with DOTween Pro and LitMotion, and much lighter than Animator and AnimationUI. Text effects are the fastest: 0.61ms for 100 texts, compared with about 2.1ms for code tweens. KeyTween makes no GC allocations during playback. For details, see Performance. Code Tweens (LitMotion, DOTween) LitMotion has the lowest cost for starting a play. However, because the effect lives in code, every preview or change requires a compile. With KeyTween you can split the two: keep the motion in the editor and set only the values that change in code with With. Animator You can author and record effects in the editor, but Animator is the heaviest option for UI effects. It lacks the following features. Per-character effects Starting from the current value

articles/en/concepts.html.title: Concepts | KeyTween
articles/en/concepts.html.summary: Concepts This guide explains how to create, preview and save animations in the KeyTween editor. The editor UI is in English, and this guide uses the names exactly as they appear on screen. This page explains the terms used throughout the KeyTween editor. The KeyTween Component KeyTween is the component that holds the animation. Add it to a prefab or a scene object, and it animates the objects under it. The animation data is serialized inside the KeyTween component, with no separate asset. As a result, the animation travels with the prefab when you duplicate or move it. Time in the component inspector decides whether playback follows Time.timeScale. The default is Scaled (it follows); set it to Unscaled for UI that must keep moving while the game is paused. For details, see Play Time. State A state is one named animation. Code plays a state by this name. Examples: Hover, Open, Close A state can contain several tracks. For details, see States. Track A track animates one property of one object. For example, the Scale of a close button is one track. For details, see Adding Tracks. Key A key is the value of a track at one point in time. As in the Unity Animation window, animating 1 → 1.2 → 1 takes three keys. For details, see Editing Keys. Arrival Arrival is how the value moves from the previous key to this one. Choose one of the following: An ease (Ease) A curve (Curve) Punch Shake For details, see Arrival. Play On Play On is the moment a state plays by itself. If you do not pick one, the state plays from code. Examples of moments you can pick: When the pointer enters On click When the component is enabled For details, see Play On.

articles/en/custom-tracks.html.title: Custom Tracks | KeyTween
articles/en/custom-tracks.html.summary: Custom Tracks You can make a track for a value that has no built-in track. Write one class that animates a component of your project, and it appears in the Add Track window for objects that have that component. Writing a Track Class Derive from KeyTweenFloatTrack<T> and implement Get, which reads the value, and Set, which writes it. T is the component the track animates. using KeyTweening; using UnityEngine.Scripting; using UnityEngine.UI; [Preserve] public sealed class ScrollbarSizeTrack : KeyTweenFloatTrack<Scrollbar> { protected override float Get(Scrollbar target) => target.size; protected override void Set(Scrollbar target, float value) => target.size = value; } The class must be public and have a parameterless constructor. Put it in a runtime assembly, not in an Editor folder, because it must also play in builds. The track's name is the class name without Track. The example above shows as Scrollbar Size. Value Types Derive from the class that matches the value. The key inspector shows a matching field. Base class Value Key field KeyTweenFloatTrack<T> float number KeyTweenVector2Track<T> Vector2 x, y KeyTweenVector3Track<T> Vector3 x, y, z KeyTweenColorTrack<T> Color color KeyTweenCustomTrack<T> Vector4 x, y, z, w Changing the Name, Color and Conditions Override these properties when you need to. Property Use Name The name shown on the track and in the Add Track window TrackColor The track's color in the timeline Range The slider range of a number track (e.g. new Vector2(0, 1)) Offers(Component) Which objects show this track (e.g. only with a certain setting) public override string Name => "Handle Size"; public override Vector2 Range => new(0f, 1f); Preview and Recording When the preview stops, the values a track changed are written back to what they were before the preview. If you list the serialized fields the value is stored in, recording also puts keys on that track. public override void SerializedFields(Component target, List<(Object owner, string path)> fields) => fields.Add((target, "m_Size")); When a Build Strips Code A track is created from its saved class name. With IL2CPP and a Managed Stripping Level above Minimal, classes that no code uses directly can be removed. Mark the class with [Preserve] to keep it. When a Class Is Renamed A track is saved with the full name of its class (namespace and assembly included). If you rename the class or its namespace, the track shows as (missing) and writes nothing. Rename it back, or add the track again.

articles/en/editing-keys.html.title: Editing Keys | KeyTween
articles/en/editing-keys.html.summary: Editing Keys A key is the value of a track at one point in time. You add and move keys on the timeline, and edit their values and arrival in the key inspector. Selecting and Moving Keys Click a key to select it. Shift-click or Ctrl-click (Cmd-click on Mac) to add to the selection. Drag on empty space in the key area to select the keys the box touches, across tracks. You can start on a track's lane, on the event and child call lanes at the top, or in the empty space below the last track. Hold Shift or Ctrl while dragging to add to the selection. Drag one of the selected keys to move all of them by the same time. One Ctrl+Z undoes it. When two or more keys at different times are selected, a box spans them. Drag its right handle to stretch or shrink the keys around the left end, or its left handle to do it around the right end; the spacing between the keys scales evenly. A handle stops before the other end, so the keys keep their order. One Ctrl+Z undoes it. Keys move in 0.01 s steps and never go below 0 s. Adding and Deleting Keys Add a key in any of these ways: Double-click an empty part of a row. The key gets the interpolated value at that time. Click ◆ on the track header. The key is added at the playhead. Right-click and choose Add Key Here. Every track has a key at 0 s. If you add a key to a track that has no 0 s key, the 0 s key is created first. To delete keys, press Delete or Backspace, or right-click and choose Delete Selected Keys. Copying and Pasting Keys Select keys and press Ctrl+C (Cmd+C on Mac). They can be on several tracks. Put the playhead where the keys should go. Press Ctrl+V (Cmd+V on Mac). Copy Selected Keys and Paste Keys at Playhead in the context menu do the same. The earliest key lands on the playhead and the spacing between the keys stays the same. Values, arrival and curves are copied too. Keys go on the track of the same object and kind as the copied ones. Pasted into another state without that track, the track is created. Pasted into the KeyTween of another prefab, keys go on the object at the same path from the root. Keys whose object is not there are skipped. The playhead does not go past the end of the state. To paste after the end, right-click there and choose Paste Keys Here. A key already at a pasted time is replaced. The pasted keys are selected, so you can drag them right away. Navigating the Timeline Action How Move the playhead Click or drag on the ruler Zoom The wheel over the ruler, or Ctrl+wheel or Alt+wheel over the rows Pan Shift+wheel, a horizontal wheel, or a middle-button drag Frame all F or ⤢ Collapse Click an object row Zooming is centered on the pointer. When an object row is collapsed, the keys under it are summarized as small diamonds. The ruler shows where the state ends (End 0.80s), and everything after that point is shaded dark. Key Inspector When you select a key, the inspector shows a Key section followed by an Arrival section. Every key uses the same layout. In the Key section, fields that do not apply are not hidden. They are disabled and show the reason. The Arrival section shows only the fields for the chosen Type. Setting a Key's Value In the Key section, set the key's Time (s) and value. The value field is labeled by what the value means, as one of the following: Value Value (rest +) Value (press point +) Value (× own size) Strength (for Punch and Shake) How you edit the value depends on its kind: Scale is edited with one linked slider (0 to 2, or −1 to 1 on a Relative To Rest track). A button switches to per-axis editing. Colors use a color field. Active uses a checkbox. Values that are decided when playback starts are disabled. For example, the first key of a track whose Start is Current Value is disabled. Setting the Arrival In the Arrival section, choose a Type and set the fields for that Type. A curve graph is shown as well. Type Fields Ease Ease Punch, Shake Ease, Frequency, Damping Curve Animation Curve Arrival is disabled on the first key, since no segment arrives at it. With several keys selected, you can change Arrival for all of them at once. For how each Type behaves, see Arrival.

articles/en/editor-window.html.title: The Editor Window | KeyTween
articles/en/editor-window.html.summary: The Editor Window The KeyTween window is where you create states and tracks, edit keys and preview the result. This page explains how to open the window and what is on screen. Opening the Window Open the window in any of these ways. The window title is "KeyTween". Choose Window > KeyTween Editor from the menu. Click Open KeyTween Editor in the KeyTween inspector. Click Edit or Create on a state row of another component. Components such as ScrollList show these buttons. The Edited Target The window edits the KeyTween on the selected object or on one of its parents. Expand Raw Data (read-only) in the inspector to see the serialized data as it is stored. It is read-only; edit states and tracks in the KeyTween Editor. Adding a KeyTween When nothing is being edited, you can add a KeyTween right from the window. Select an object in the Hierarchy. It does not have to be a UI object (a SpriteRenderer, a 3D object and so on). Click the Add KeyTween to 'name' button that appears in the window. If another KeyTween is already being edited, the window keeps that target. In that case, add the component with Add Component instead. Window Layout The window is divided into the top bar, the state tabs, the timeline on the left and the inspector on the right. Area Contents Top bar The target name, playback and recording, and saving controls State tabs One tab per state Timeline (left) Track rows grouped by object hierarchy, the ruler and the state end (End) mark Inspector (right) Settings for the selected item A state tab's tooltip shows that state's Play On. The + tab adds a state. The inspector's contents change depending on whether you selected a state, track, key, event, sound or child call. The Top Bar The top bar has the following controls. Control Function ▶ Play and pause ■ Stop. Returns to the original values ⟲ Loop ● Record Speed 0.1x, 0.25x, 0.5x, 1x Time The current time and length Auto Save, Save Saving Orange dot Shown when unsaved values are on screen For details, see Saving and Recording.

articles/en/events-and-sounds.html.title: Events and Sounds | KeyTween
articles/en/events-and-sounds.html.summary: Events and Sounds A state can signal your code or play a sound at a set time. Both are added as tracks from the Add Track window. Use them to keep the game logic in time with the motion. For example, put a Hit event at 0.3 s of a sword swing (the moment the blade lands), and the code deals the damage and spawns the particles then. When the keys move, you move the event with them; there is no wait time in the code to fix. Adding an Event Choose Animation Events in the Add Track window. An event track is created. Click + on the track header, or double-click the row. Choose Name Only or a data struct in the menu, and the event is created. In the inspector, set the Name and Time (s). The kind can be changed later in the Event Type section below them. Drag an event to move it. Event Type The Type is one of the following: Name Only A struct marked with [KeyTweenEvent] in code When you choose a struct, you can edit its fields right in the inspector. These field types can be edited: float, int, bool, string Vector2/3 Color enum Receiving Events Receive events in either of these ways: In code. For details, see API. anim.EventRaised += (in KeyTweenEventInfo e) => { if (e.Name == "Hit") DealDamage(); }; await anim.WaitEventAsync("Hit"); // or wait for it once With the KeyTween Event Listener component, which connects a UnityEvent to each event name. Adding a Sound Choose Sound in the Add Track window. A sound track is created. Click + on the track header, double-click the row, or drop an AudioClip onto the row to add a sound. In the inspector, set the Clip, Volume and Time. Click ▶ Preview to listen to it. The length of the bar on the timeline matches the length of the clip. Which AudioSource Plays the Sound The sound plays through the first AudioSource found in this order, so you do not need to add an AudioSource to every UI object: Audio Source (optional) in the sound track's inspector KeyTween.audioSource, set in code (it cannot be edited in the inspector) If neither exists, a hidden shared 2D AudioSource Sounds and State Length The state's length includes the end of the sound. As a result, the sound is not cut off when you Destroy the object after a close animation ends.

articles/en/installation.html.title: Installation | KeyTween
articles/en/installation.html.summary: Installation This section explains how to install KeyTween in your project. Requirements Unity 6000.0 or later Installed along with KeyTween com.unity.ugui 2.0.0 (includes TextMeshPro) com.unity.mathematics 1.3.2 com.unity.burst 1.8.25 Install via Package Manager (Recommended) Install KeyTween from its Git URL in the Package Manager. Open Window > Package Manager. Click the + button and select Add package from git URL.... Enter the following URL: https://github.com/UnialGames/KeyTween.git Alternatively, add the following line to the dependencies block of Packages/manifest.json: { "dependencies": { "com.unialgames.keytween": "https://github.com/UnialGames/KeyTween.git" } } Updating The URL above always points to the latest release. When a new version is out, select KeyTween in the Package Manager and click Update. Installing a specific version Add # and a version tag to the URL to stay on that version. All versions are listed on the Releases page. https://github.com/UnialGames/KeyTween.git#v0.3.0 A pinned version does not change when you click Update. To change the version, edit the tag in Packages/manifest.json. To follow the latest release again, remove #v… from the URL. Importing samples Select KeyTween in the Package Manager. Open the Samples tab and click Import next to a sample. Samples are copied into your project. After updating the package, import them again to get the new version.

articles/en/nested-prefabs.html.title: Nested Prefabs | KeyTween
articles/en/nested-prefabs.html.summary: Nested Prefabs These features are for a shared prefab, such as a button, placed inside another prefab, such as a popup. Child call: the popup's state calls the button's state. Override: changes the button's animation only inside the popup. Adding a Child Call A child call plays a state of a child prefab at a set time in the parent state. Double-click an object row, or right-click and choose Add Child Call ▸ child ▸ state. Drag the bar that appears on the parent's timeline to change its time. In the inspector, set the Child, State and Time. States that are already called are checked and cannot be chosen. How Child Calls Play The parent state's length includes call time + child state length. Calling Complete on the parent brings the child to its end values as well. If the parent is canceled, a child that has already started keeps playing. Cycles of states calling each other are cut off at depth 8. Overriding a Track An override changes the child's animation per track, and only inside the current prefab. Under a child call, the child state's tracks are shown shifted by the call time. The original tracks are dimmed and read-only. Click a dimmed track under the child call. Only that track is overridden. Edit its keys. The edits go into the override, and the original prefab is not changed. In the screenshot below, Popup's Open state calls OkButton's Hover at 0.2 s and overrides OkButton's Color track inside the popup only. The overridden Color track has a blue name and an ×. The Scale track, not overridden, is dimmed. The child call's heading shows how many tracks are overridden and a ↺. Editing the Original Prefab Overrides are saved in the outer prefab's own KeyTween. Only the changed tracks are saved, so when you edit other tracks in the original, the popup picks up those changes. In the original prefab Overridden track Track not overridden Change key values or times The popup keeps its values The popup follows Add a track — It appears in the popup too Delete a track It stays in the popup It is removed from the popup too Overrides on Several Levels When several levels, such as screen > popup > button, override the same track, the outermost level wins. This is the same rule as Unity's nested prefabs. Overridden tracks have blue names. Their tooltip shows which prefab overrides them. Reverting Overrides Control What it reverts × on a track The outermost level of that track's override ↺ on the child call title All overrides at the outermost level (like Unity's Revert All) Inspector › Overrides › Revert Overrides made on a scene instance

articles/en/other-components.html.title: Sounds, Selection and Other Components | KeyTween
articles/en/other-components.html.summary: Sounds, Selection and Other Components Sound Source This setting decides which AudioSource plays the sounds of sound tracks. Choosing the AudioSource Set it in code with KeyTween.audioSource. The inspector does not edit this field (it shows only under Raw Data). If it is set, sounds play through that source. If it is empty, sounds play through one shared, hidden 2D AudioSource (PlayOneShot). You only need to set it when you need a mixer group or 3D sound. Each sound track can also set its own source. Optional Integrations When the following libraries are installed, KeyTween gains extra extension methods. Library Extension methods UniTask PlayUniTaskAsync, PlayReversedUniTaskAsync, WaitEventUniTaskAsync R3 PlayAsObservable, EventsAsObservable, EventAsObservable, StateStartedAsObservable, StateCompletedAsObservable, StateCanceledAsObservable An integration turns on automatically when its library is installed, with nothing to configure. The same methods also take a start time, and work on a With play. For details, see Integrations. Other Components Besides KeyTween, the package provides the following components. articles/en/overlapping-states.html.title: When States Overlap | KeyTween
articles/en/overlapping-states.html.summary: When States Overlap Several states can play at the same time. For example, pressing a button while it is hovered plays both states together. Taking Over Properties The new state takes over only the properties it animates from the earlier state, right where they are. The earlier state keeps playing the rest. A state that has handed over all of its properties stops, and its PlayAsync is canceled. Tracks whose Start is Current Value continue from where they stopped. This is why a hover that is cut short does not jump. Tracks That Write the Same Value Tracks of different kinds that write the same value take over only the part they share (the channels). Tracks that write the same value Shared channels Color and Alpha (Graphic, SpriteRenderer) transparency (a) Char Color and Char Alpha transparency (a) Position, Size and Offset Min, Offset Max (RectTransform) the position and size an offset changes Position and World Position, Rotation and World Rotation all of it For example, when a button's Hover plays Color and Fade then plays Alpha: Hover keeps writing R, G and B. Fade takes the transparency. The other way round, when Hover starts during Fade, Fade has handed over its only channel, so it stops. Finishing the Earlier State First Sometimes the earlier state must reach its end pose and raise its events before the next one plays. In that case, call Complete("earlier state") from code first, then play the next state. anim.Complete("Hover"); // moves the earlier state to its end pose anim.Play("Press"); For details, see API.

articles/en/performance.html.title: Performance | KeyTween
articles/en/performance.html.summary: Performance This page shows how KeyTween performs compared with Animator, DOTween and LitMotion, and what to keep in mind when you use it. The values were measured on 2026-10-15~16. All result tables: Benchmarks.md 1. Conclusion This section sums up the results measured with an IL2CPP release build and 2,000 objects. Results The values in parentheses show the time above setting the same values directly from a script (the baseline), which is the cost of the method itself. KeyTween DOTween Pro LitMotion Animator AnimationUI Looping pulse (ms) 7.69 (+0.38) 7.71 (+0.40) 7.66 (+0.34) 10.16 (+2.85) 9.31 (+2.00) List entry (ms) 1.70 (+0.04) 1.59 (−0.06) 1.53 (−0.13) 5.23 (+3.57) 2.18 (+0.52) Text wave, 100 objects (ms) 0.61 2.11 2.05 not supported not supported GC per frame (vs. baseline) 0 pulse 0, entry +11KB 0 +0.1KB +16KB These values come from a single run, so each case varies by about ±5%. Differences of less than 0.1ms between methods are within that range. Strengths Faster than Animator and AnimationUI. With 2,000 pulses, KeyTween's own cost is about 1/5 to 1/7 of theirs (+0.38ms vs. +2.0~2.9ms). On par with code tweens. With 2,000 pulses, KeyTween is within 0.05ms of DOTween Pro (+0.40) and LitMotion (+0.34). Code tweens are libraries such as DOTween and LitMotion, in which effects are written in code. Text effects are the fastest. With 100 texts, KeyTween takes about 1/3 of the time of DOTween Pro and LitMotion. No GC allocation during playback. By contrast, DOTween allocates on every replay (11KB per frame for 2,000 list entries). AnimationUI also allocates every time because of its coroutines. Weak Spot: Starting a Play This is the time it takes to restart 2,000 objects at once in list entry. KeyTween: 2.31ms LitMotion: 1.34ms DOTween: 3.89ms It only becomes noticeable when thousands of plays start in the same frame. For details, see The Cost of Starting a Play below. Why List Entry Shows Negative Values The negative values in list entry, which are faster than the baseline, come from how the measurement works. The baseline script keeps setting values every frame after the effect ends, while the libraries stop after 0.4 s. During that period the baseline does more work, so values near 0 should be read as "no difference". 2. Method All methods were compared under the same conditions. How Methods Are Compared The same effect is applied to the same objects (N images, N texts) with each method. Looping pulse List entry (played again every 0.5 s) Text wave The baseline (direct set) uses no animation system: one script sets the same values every frame. uGUI's redraw cost is the same in every method, so the difference from the baseline is the cost of each method. Environment Windows 64-bit player, 1280×720 windowed VSync off, no frame limit For each case, a 1 s warm-up, then every frame recorded for 4 s CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D Unity: 6000.6.3f1 Time and GC Time: frame times of release builds (Mono, IL2CPP) GC: measured separately with a development build. The allocation counter (GC Allocated In Frame) works only in development builds. 3. What to Know When Using It These points affect performance on screens that use many KeyTweens. Cost When Not Playing A KeyTween that is not playing does nothing each frame. Even with many KeyTweens on screen, only the ones that are playing cost anything. GC Allocation While Playing Playing allocates no GC memory. This holds for looping states and for playing the same state again and again, and for states with child calls. The exception is a state that calls a child state whose tracks an outer prefab overrides. Each time such a state plays, working out its length merges the overridden child state anew. With and Build With(state) and Build(state) make new objects each time they are called. So calling With(...) again for every play allocates that much. Keep the KeyTweenPlay that With returns in a field and play it again. Reused, it allocates nothing when it plays. Call Build once to make the state, then play it with Play("name"). Tracks Evaluated with Burst Tracks whose keys all use ease presets are gathered and evaluated together, in one Burst call for all playing tracks. The following tracks are evaluated one by one in managed code, so they are a little slower: AnimationCurve keys Punch and Shake keys Per-character tracks Random-character (scramble) reveal If you put the same effect on thousands of objects, building it with ease presets is faster. com.unity.burst is installed along with KeyTween for this. The Cost of Starting a Play Starting a play packs its keys for the Burst evaluation. Playing 2,000 again in one frame takes 2.31ms on IL2CPP. On a normal screen this does not show. If you start thousands in the same frame, spread them over a few frames. Text Effects A text with per-character tracks is not laid out again every frame; only the per-character changes are applied to the first layout. It is laid out again only when: The text, size, color or number of visible characters changes The number of characters changes The text box size changes Changing the text often while it plays costs a layout each time. Allocation on First Use The first time a KeyTween plays, it reserves arrays for the Burst evaluation once. For 2,000 states this is about 1.2–1.4MB; after that, playing allocates nothing. The setup allocation in the benchmarks (about 6.6MB for 2,000 KeyTweens) is a different number, because that measurement includes making the states in code.

articles/en/play-on.html.title: Play On | KeyTween
articles/en/play-on.html.summary: Play On Play On sets when a state plays by itself, without code. Choosing Play On Select the state tab to show the state inspector. Choose an event from the Play On list. Choosing an event adds a KeyTweenTrigger component automatically. When Each Option Plays Play On Plays when None The state does not play by itself. Play it from code with Play or PlayAsync OnEnable The component is enabled Start Once, after the component is first enabled PointerEnter / PointerExit / PointerDown / PointerUp / Click The matching pointer event occurs Select / Deselect The matching selection event occurs ToggleOn / ToggleOff The value of the Toggle on the same object changes For playing from code, see API. Example: A Hover Button A button that grows when the mouse is over it and shrinks back when it leaves takes two states. A Hover state: a Scale track from 1 to 1.08, with Play On set to PointerEnter. An Unhover state: a Scale track from 1.08 to 1, with Play On set to PointerExit. Set Start to Current Value on both tracks, so that if the mouse leaves while the button is still growing, it shrinks back from where it is. No code is needed. When the moment depends on the game (the score changed, a screen opened), leave Play On at None and play the state from code. Things to Note A warning appears when two states would play at the same moment. For example, OnEnable and Start are both called on Instantiate. A Selectable whose interactable is off ignores input events. OnEnable and Start still play in that case. Pointer events come from the EventSystem. For an object that is not UI (a SpriteRenderer, a 3D object) to get them, the camera needs a Physics2DRaycaster or PhysicsRaycaster and the object a Collider. Playing from a UnityEvent You can also play a state from a UnityEvent, such as a Button's OnClick. Choose KeyTween.Play (string) in the function list. Enter the state name. To play it in reverse, choose PlayReversed (string).

articles/en/playing-and-awaiting.html.title: Playing and Awaiting | KeyTween
articles/en/playing-and-awaiting.html.summary: Playing and Awaiting KeyTween lives in the KeyTweening namespace, and the component you add to a GameObject is KeyTween. Animations are made in the editor as states (Guide). A state is one named animation, built from tracks and keys. From code, you play a state by name and await it. The KeyTween component provides methods to play and control a state by its name. public sealed class KeyTween : MonoBehaviour { public void Play(string stateName); // takes one argument, so it is also listed in UnityEvents such as Button OnClick public void Play(string stateName, PointerEventData pointer); // for Start = Pointer tracks (where the pointer was pressed) public void Play(string stateName, float time); // plays from that time (seconds) public Awaitable PlayAsync(string stateName, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default); public Awaitable PlayAsync(string stateName, float time, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default); public void PlayReversed(string stateName); // also listed in UnityEvents public void PlayReversed(string stateName, float time); // from that time back to 0 s public Awaitable PlayReversedAsync(string stateName, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default); public Awaitable PlayReversedAsync(string stateName, float time, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default); public void Complete(string stateName); // jumps a playing state to its end public void Stop(string stateName); // stops the state where it is public void Stop(string stateName, float time); // stops it and shows the pose at that time (without playing) public KeyTweenPlay With(string stateName); // sets up one play in code ("Setting Up a Play in Code") public KeyTweenStateBuilder Build(string stateName); // makes a state in code ("Making a State in Code") public bool IsPlaying(string stateName); public bool HasState(string stateName); public float Duration(string stateName); // length including overrides; 0 if there is no such state } Method Behavior Play Starts playing. With a time, plays from that time. PlayAsync Starts playing and waits until the play ends. PlayReversed Plays from the end (or the given time) back to the start. Complete Jumps a playing state to its end pose. Stop Stops the state where it is. With a time, stops it and shows the pose at that time. Times are in seconds on the state's timeline (the same unit as Duration). A time below 0 or past the length is clamped to 0 or the end. Playing a State Play starts playing and writes the first pose (0 s) immediately. If the state name does not exist, it only logs a warning. anim.Play("Open"); If the state has Start = Pointer tracks, also pass pointer. The tracks use it to know where the pointer was pressed. public void OnPointerDown(PointerEventData eventData) => anim.Play("Press", eventData); Awaiting a Play PlayAsync completes when the play reaches the end or when Complete is called. await anim.PlayAsync("Open", destroyCancellationToken); If the play cannot finish, it ends with OperationCanceledException. For details, see How a Play Ends. If the state does not exist, it completes immediately. It returns a Unity Awaitable, so you can await it only once. For a looping state, PlayAsync does not end until you call Complete or Stop. Playing from a Given Time Pass a time to Play or PlayAsync to play from that time. The pose at that time is written at once, and only the rest of the state plays. anim.Play("Intro", 1.5f); // from 1.5 s await anim.PlayAsync("Intro", 1.5f, destroyCancellationToken); Events, sounds and child calls before that time are not raised. Those exactly at the start time are raised, as those at 0 s are when playing from 0 s. Pass a time to PlayReversed or PlayReversedAsync to play from that time back toward 0 s. Playing in Reverse PlayReversed plays from the end back to the start. To wait until it ends, use PlayReversedAsync. await anim.PlayReversedAsync("Open"); // returns to where the forward play started Events, sounds and child calls are each raised once, in reverse order. Child states also play reversed. Start = Current Value tracks reuse the value captured by the last forward play. So a reversed play returns exactly to where the forward play started. The end values are also those of the last forward play. If the forward play was With(...).WithEndValue(...), a plain PlayReversed comes back from that end value. To give a reversed play another end value, use With(...).WithEndValue(...).PlayReversed(). Completing a Play Complete moves a playing state to its end pose and completes PlayAsync normally. It works only while the state is playing. anim.Complete("Open"); The remaining events and child calls are raised in order. Remaining sounds are not played. During a reversed play, it moves to the start pose instead. Stopping a Play Stop stops the state where it is. A pending PlayAsync is canceled. Use it to turn off a looping state. anim.Stop("Idle"); Stopping at a Given Time Pass a time to Stop to stop the state if it is playing (a pending PlayAsync is canceled) and write its pose at that time. It writes the pose even when the state is not playing. anim.Stop("Open", anim.Duration("Open")); // straight to the end pose, without animation anim.Stop("Reveal", progress * anim.Duration("Reveal")); // every frame from a value such as a scroll position (progress: 0 to 1) No timer runs, and no events or sounds are raised. You can call it every frame to drive the pose with something other than time, such as a scroll position or a pull distance.
